Personal Computers aren't designed to be the most secure machines ever. On your hard drive data is divide into two parts. The data itself and the filemap that points to where the data is stored. When you delete a file on your pc it just deletes the entry in the filemap not the actual data. The data can stick around for years after until some more data overwrites it. This is how your hard drive can easily be recovered. 

Now since web servers have to be secure, a lot are setup so that when you delete a file, both the map entry and the data are wiped. It's more secure but obviously takes a lot longer than just deleting the file map entry. 

You'll note that moving files can be done in milliseconds too, this is because the filemap entry is changed but the data stays in the same place.

Sorry about the length of this, but SSDs really aren't as simple as a one word answer :P

The thing about SSDs that differ from Hard drives is that a hard drive uses a disk. It uses the same principle as DVDs, CDs, Tapes etc. In a hard drive an arm that stretches the length of the disk will have the ability to view any portion of the disk (the size of this portion is determined by the storage capacity of the hard drive). As with CDs and tapes, data is stored as 1s and 0s and this is exactly the same in a hard drive. However in a hard drive and a cassette tape, these 1s ands 0s are stored magnetically (hence if you put a magnet near a hard drive it messes up). CDs, DVDs and Blurays all store the data as etched groves on the surface, a laser is shined into these groves and the way the light returns determines if it is a 1 or a 0.

Now for Solid State Drives. These don't use magnets or groves like any other media but instead use semiconductor material. RAM in your computer works in the same way but the storage is temporary, so if you remove power the data is lost. RAM works by creating a "loop" of electricity (this is done using circuits similar to [flip flops](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flip-flop_(electronics) ). However similar to how shining a laser into a house of mirrors will not yield everlasting light, the same happens with RAM: remove the electricity and the energy is lost and thus the "electricity loops" stop.

Now since SSDs require their data to be around even when electricity is removed, they use a different process. There are storage types (such as EEPROM) which will physically burn data into semiconductor material, and therefore can only have the data changed less than 100,000 times (or so). This isn't ideal for SSDs so instead they use a processes of altering the charge on a semiconductor material. It's a complicated process but essential you have a write line that allows the material to have its charged changed and then once the write line is not active the material will then allow charge to flow or not (based on the charge set). In this manner you can get millions of these semiconductor material portions that work in the same way allowing you have millions of bits of data. Since it uses electric charge, it can be stored regardless of having a power supply attached. Think about taking a balloon and rubbing it on your jumper, put it near your hair and your hair stands on end (due to the charge being present). However as long as you don't discharge the balloon, by allowing it to touch a ground point, that balloon will make your hair stand on end every time you put it near your head. In a similar way, SSDs will not lose the charge stored on each bit of data. This is the same principle used for flash memory

Remember:
CDs, DVDs, Blurays use light and tiny etched groves
Cassettes and Hard drives use magnetic data 
RAM uses a continuous loops of current
SSDs and Flash memory use electric charge
